title: Bedtime prayers
hook: Now I lay me down to sleep: children's prayers carried for life

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace at meals, said by one family so fast it came out as one long word. Your line was these thy gifts. Before which bite did you stop for a breath? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

The bedroom light is off. Only the hallway lamp is on, and the door is open a crack. A small voice comes from under a blanket, rushing a little: "Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep." A parent sits on the edge of the bed and says it along. Years go by. The child grows up, moves away, stops saying it. Then one night, in a strange bed, a hospital, a hotel, the night before something hard, the words come back on their own, word for word, as if they'd been waiting. Today: bedtime prayers.
screen: `NOW I LAY ME DOWN TO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Start with the children's prayer itself. In its old form it goes: "Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep; If I should die before I wake, I pray the Lord my soul to take." It isn't a Bible verse. It's an old children's prayer, and its third line can startle a modern parent. Some families keep it. Some swap in a gentler line. Either way, the heart of it is the same: before letting go of the day, a child hands themselves over to God's keeping. Next, the Psalms. One psalm carries a heading that sets it when David fled from Absalom, his own son, and it says: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." Enemies all around, and he sleeps. Another psalm ends: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Lying down becomes an act of trust. Then, the one who doesn't sleep. Psalm one hundred twenty-one says: "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." That's the quiet logic of a bedtime prayer. You can close your eyes because someone else is keeping watch. Last, the grown-up version. The old English prayer book gives the whole church a prayer for evening: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night." Same request as the child under the blanket, in longer words. Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants each have their own night prayers, short or long, said alone or together. And for some, the children's prayer is still the one that comes first in the dark: keep me through the night.
screen: `NOW I LAY ME DOWN TO SLEEP.`
`I LAID ME DOWN AND SLEPT; I AWAKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a bedtime prayer. If it's night, lie down. If it isn't, sit back and let your shoulders drop as if it were. Settle, and breathe. Let the day go, one piece at a time: the conversations, the tasks, the thing you didn't finish. If you pray, you can say the children's prayer, or the psalm on the screen, slowly, the way you'd hand something to someone you trust. If you don't, simply notice what it would feel like to set the whole day down and let someone else keep watch. The bell holds the time.
screen: `I WILL BOTH LAY ME DOWN IN PEACE, AND SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Bedtime prayers. The words said before sleep, handing the night over to God's keeping, sometimes learned as a child and kept for life.
Your line: keep me through the night. Tonight, before you sleep, take one slow breath and let the day go before you close your eyes. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Some Christian parents teach children a short prayer to say at bedtime, such as "Now I lay me down to sleep"; Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants also have longer evening and night prayers, said at home or in church.

fork.setup: you're David, running from your own son's army. enemies are all around, and night is falling. what do you do?
options: stay awake on guard all night.
fork.reveal: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." sleep, in the psalm, is an act of trust.

original.note: Hebrew: keeper, one who watches over. Psalm 121's "he that keepeth Israel."

trapdoor: what you thought: a bedtime prayer is a rhyme for little kids.
what it means: handing yourself over to God's keeping before you let go of the day.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 121's shomer, the keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps. you can close your eyes because someone else is awake.
